plan.topic: Is nausea a sign tirzepatide is working? Correcting the myth with label and trial evidence
plan.angle: Sentence 1: 'Is tirzepatide nausea a sign it's working? Here's what the trials show.' By 6 s: nausea is a common side effect reported by a minority on each dose vs placebo (label pooled rates, with the pooled studies named). In a SURPASS analysis of adults with type 2 diabetes, weight loss was similar with or without nausea (DOM 2024). Then the tips, the emergency card, the scoped don't-stop line, 'Not personal advice', the prescriber line and the closing line.
plan.working_title: Tirzepatide Nausea: Does It Mean It's Working? #shorts
plan.why:
Funnels to Side Effects, our top Lane A long video. It's a felt symptom with proven Short demand (180 views), and the myth framing is a new angle, not a repeat of the 10-24 'why it happens' Short. | fact-check: This is a useful positive myth-bust. Fixes:
(a) The hook 'doesn't mean it's working better' is a causal claim. A post hoc analysis supports it, but only in type 2 diabetes. In the SURPASS 1–5 trials (N=6,263), mean weight reduction was similar whether or not people reported nausea, vomiting or diarrhea, and the mediation analysis put the GI events' contribution at under 6% (Patel et al., Diabetes Obes Metab 2024, PubMed 37853960). If you use it, name the population: adults with type 2 diabetes in the SURPASS trials. Don't extend it to SURMOUNT unless a SURMOUNT analysis is cited.
(b) The Zepbound label's nausea rates pool more than one trial, so don't call them 'SURMOUNT-1' rates. Use the label's pooled per-arm rates with the label's own description of the pooled studies. For SURMOUNT-1 alone, use the NEJM 2022 (Jastreboff) per-arm rates.
(c) Replace 'most people lost weight on average' with the mean percentage weight change by dose vs placebo.

package.title: Tirzepatide Nausea: Sign It's Working? #shorts
package.description:
Tirzepatide nausea: a sign it's working? Not necessarily. In SURPASS trials in adults with type 2 diabetes, mean weight loss was similar with or without nausea, vomiting or diarrhea.

Severe stomach pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting? Stop and call your healthcare provider right away. For anything that isn't that emergency sign, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.

Patel et al., Diabetes Obes Metab 2024: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37853960/

#tirzepatide #GLP1
Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

factcheck.summary: The core claims hold up against the sources. On the label numbers: the Zepbound PI (revised 8/2026, DailyMed) lists nausea at 25%, 29% and 28% for 5, 10 and 15 mg versus 8% on placebo in pooled Studies 1 and 2. On the study: Patel et al. exists as cited (Diabetes Obes Metab 2024;26(2):473–481, PMID 37853960, SURPASS-1 to -5, N=6,263, type 2 diabetes). Its abstract says mean weight loss was consistent whether or not people reported nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea. It also says these side effects explained less than 6% of the weight difference between tirzepatide and its comparators. The type 2 diabetes population is named in the narration, so the move from the obesity label to the diabetes trials is handled correctly. The emergency card matches the label's pancreatitis warning, the safety lines are in the required order, and the closing line is right for the 20:00 slot. The script is 157 spoken words (I counted), inside the standard arm. Only four minor wording fixes remain: one approximation that's slightly generous, two on-screen cards that drop scope, and an optional fluids tip. I couldn't confirm the meal tip ('simple meals, skip rich or spicy food') on the NHS tirzepatide page. It's untagged general advice worded as 'may help', so it can stay.

issues.claim: So about three in four didn't.
issues.problem: 25–29% reporting nausea means 71–75% didn't. At the 10 mg and 15 mg doses (29%, 28%) that's closer to seven in ten than three in four, so the rounding is slightly generous.
issues.fix: Replace with: "So more than seven in ten didn't." (6 words, same count; spoken total stays at 157)

issues.claim: Under 6% of tirzepatide's extra weight loss
issues.problem: A muted viewer can't tell what the 6% means: the card doesn't say it's the share explained by GI side effects, and it leaves out the type 2 diabetes population. It could be misread as 'only 6% extra weight loss'.
issues.fix: on_screen_text: "GI side effects explained under 6% of the extra weight loss (type 2 diabetes trials)"

issues.problem: The card drops the population (adults with type 2 diabetes, SURPASS), which the narration includes.
issues.fix: on_screen_text: "Type 2 diabetes trials: weight loss similar either way"

issues.claim: Small, simple meals and skipping rich or spicy food may help.
issues.problem: Optional. The label warns that fluid loss from GI side effects can lead to dehydration and kidney problems. A fluids tip would be a helpful addition and still fits the word budget.
issues.fix: Narration: "Small, simple meals, skipping rich or spicy food, and sipping fluids may help." (spoken total 160; if you also use the S3-2 fix it stays at 160). Add "Sip fluids" as a 4th list item.
